domain: Institutional economics and mechanism design — principal-agent theory, moral hazard, audit independence, and Goodhart-aware incentive design as applied to delegated technical work such as QA/dev separation, CI gate design, SRE error-budget incentives, and compensation-metric gaming
axioms: Any party whose actions are costly to observe directly — an executor's actual effort, an orchestrator's plan-writing thoroughness — will be judged by proxies, and will rationally respond to the proxy's incentive gradient rather than to the principal's unstated true goal.

An auditor is only as independent as its selection, funding, and criteria-setting are separated from the party being audited; an auditor checking work against a rubric written by the auditee is auditing compliance with the auditee's own standard, not correctness.

Moral hazard exists wherever an agent bears less than the full cost of its own failures — a fresh-context executor with no stake beyond the current task has structurally weaker incentive to invest effort in flagging ambiguity than a principal who owns the consequences.

A rule with an unmonitored escape hatch degrades toward the exception over time under schedule pressure, at a rate proportional to how costly compliance is and how unlikely detection is — this is assumed as a default trajectory, not merely a possibility.

Escalation and governance decisions need a decision-owner distinct from the party whose prior attempt is being escalated; a self-escalating party has an inherent conflict of interest in judging when escalation is warranted.

Incentive-compatibility must be checked at the level of the metric an actor is actually scored against, not the goal the metric was designed to approximate — the two are assumed to diverge until proven otherwise.

A metric's own definitions are themselves a governed asset; if no one owns keeping them honest, they drift toward whatever makes the metric easiest to satisfy, independent of any single actor's intent to game them.
primitives: principal (the orchestrator, and the human doctrine owner behind it)
agent (the executor, delegated narrow-scope work under a proxy metric)
auditor (the validator, and its independence or lack thereof from the plan's author)
incentive / metric (the token-share gate, the two-strikes counter, as things actors are scored against)
moral hazard (weak incentive to flag ambiguity when the cost of pushing through lands elsewhere)
escape hatch (the explicit `model: inherit` exception to closed spawn inheritance)
decision-owner (who is authorized to call frontier-in-the-loop escalation, and whether that party is conflicted)
failure_mode: Reads every gap as an incentive-design gap and defaults to 'name an owner' or 'add oversight' as the fix even where the real problem is a coordination or mechanics bug — a race condition, a stale read — that no amount of owner-naming would prevent; it can over-attribute intent to what is actually an infrastructure failure.

Assumes actors respond to incentive gradients in ways detectable by economic reasoning, but has no native tools to evaluate whether a judge's criteria are epistemically complete or a metric's construct validity holds, and can mistake a good-faith measurement error for a strategic one.

Leans toward game-theoretic worst-case framing — assume defection is likely — which can overstate risk in a small, high-trust pilot phase where the 'actors' are memoryless, single-shot LLM subagents without persistent stakes across runs; the repeated-game assumptions underlying classical principal-agent theory apply less cleanly here than to human organizations.

Is weak at reasoning about pure state-synchronization failures (staleness, idempotency, partial application) that have no incentive component at all — a fully honest, non-strategic executor can still apply a plan to a stale tree, and this lens has little to say about that case.
